meta.ogDescription: Not Martin Luther King Jr. It is Martin Luther the reformer, from his Table Talk (no. CCXCVIII) — a name-confusion mix-up.

answer.label: Not Martin Luther King Jr. — actually Martin Luther, the reformer
answer.authorDates: 1483–1546 · German theologian & leader of the Protestant Reformation
answer.sourceLine: The line is genuine, but it is not Dr. King’s — it belongs to Martin Luther, the 16th-century reformer, and comes from his Table Talk (Tischreden), section CCXCVIII. It continues: “No husbandman would sow one grain of corn, if he hoped not it would grow up and become seed… no merchant or tradesman would set himself to work, if he did not hope to reap benefit thereby.” The credit to Martin Luther King Jr. is a name-confusion mix-up.

source.heading: Where it really comes from

docMeta.dd: 1566, compiled by Johannes Aurifaber, in German
English by William Hazlitt, 1848 (reissued in Bohn’s Standard Library, 1857)

source.excerpt: Everything that is done in the world is done by hope. No husbandman would sow one grain of corn, if he hoped not it would grow up and become seed; no bachelor would marry a wife, if he hope not to have children; no merchant or tradesman would set himself to work, if he did not hope to reap benefit thereby, etc. How much more, then, does hope urge us on to everlasting life and salvation?
trail: The full paragraph — “Everything that is done in the world is done by hope… no merchant or tradesman would set himself to work, if he did not hope to reap benefit thereby” — sits at section CCXCVIII of Luther’s Table Talk.
The line is a compilation from Luther’s dinner-table conversations, first gathered and published in German as Tischreden in 1566, then Englished by William Hazlitt the Younger in 1848.
Reference sites file the exact wording under Martin Luther, citing the 1857 Table Talk edition, not Martin Luther King Jr.

author.name: Martin Luther
author.heading: About Martin Luther
author.metaLine: 1483–1546 · German theologian & leader of the Protestant Reformation
author.bio: Martin Luther was a German monk, theologian, and the pivotal figure of the Protestant Reformation, whose 1517 Ninety-five Theses challenged the sale of indulgences and split Western Christianity. His Table Talk (Tischreden) is not a book he wrote but a posthumous collection of his informal remarks, jotted down by students and dinner guests and first published in 1566. He is a wholly different person from the American civil-rights leader Martin Luther King Jr., born four centuries later.

misattribution.heading: How it got pinned on the wrong Luther
misattribution.intro: This is one of the internet’s most predictable mix-ups: two famous men named Luther, four centuries apart. The words are the reformer’s; the face on the graphic is often Dr. King’s.

items.why: Quote graphics and listicles routinely append “Martin Luther King” to the line, as on this posted image, because “Martin Luther” and “Martin Luther King” are so easily conflated. There is no such line in King’s sermons, speeches, or books.

misattribution.truthLine: The sentence is Martin Luther’s, from Table Talk no. CCXCVIII — the 16th-century reformer, not the 20th-century civil-rights leader.

context.heading: Why it matters
lead: In the Table Talk, Luther uses the line to make a theological point, not a motivational one: if ordinary human effort — sowing, marrying, trading — is powered by hope of a future reward, then how much more should hope drive the believer toward “everlasting life and salvation.” The quote-card version strips away the sermon and keeps only the aphorism, which is part of how the attribution drifts.
context.pull: “How much more, then, does hope urge us on to everlasting life and salvation?”
